## What was wrong

I measured the live deployment and the recent CI runs before touching anything.

**Reads were already fine.** Against `cachet.nox.so` from Vancouver: narinfo 39 ms warm / 133 ms cold, NAR at 38-42 MB/s. cache.nixos.org measures 133 ms and 50 MB/s from the same laptop. The edge cache worked, 404s cached, and curl sends Basic preemptively so the missing `WWW-Authenticate` cost no round trip.

**Reads felt slow because the cache was empty.** Of 300 random local store paths, cachet held 12 (4%); cache.nixos.org held 71. cachet is priority 30, so nix asks it first for every path in every closure, eats a 404, and goes upstream anyway.

**The cache was empty because writes were catastrophic.** From CI run 32803263823:

| Job | Build | Push |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `openapi` | 47 s | **31 min** (974 paths) |
| `wasm` | 1 m 49 s | **18 min** (830 paths) |

1.34 seconds per object. The push step was forty times the job it exists to accelerate, and pushes that slow do not finish.

## The three costs

**The worker read every NAR back to verify it.** `put_narinfo` did `head()`, then a full `bucket.get()` of the object the client uploaded minutes earlier, then a SHA-256 over the compressed bytes, a ruzstd decode, and a second SHA-256 over every decompressed byte. For rustc: 132 MB re-read, 409 MB decoded, 541 MB hashed, in wasm, per path, three times over on a client retry.

The bytes are now measured by the write that stores them, streaming through the same hashers on their way into the bucket, and the result lands beside the object as a facts document. The narinfo request reads a few hundred bytes instead of a few hundred megabytes. Verify-then-sign is unchanged — `VerifiedNar::verify` takes the same four measured values and the signer still accepts nothing else (ADR 0012). Multipart measures on completion, because its parts arrive out of order; that is the one read-back left, and only objects past 90 MiB reach it.

**The client compressed closures it then threw away.** `nix copy --to file://` staged each survivor's whole closure into a tempdir, so members the cache already held were serialized and compressed at full cost and filtered out afterwards. Each path is now serialized and compressed on its own: `nix store dump-path` streamed through a zstd encoder, hashed as it passes, held in memory below 8 MiB and spilled to one scratch file above. The narinfo is built from `nix path-info --json` rather than copied out of a staging tree.

**Uploads were barriered waves with multipart outside them.** `pipeline.rs:412` was a plain sequential `for` loop over every multipart object, so the fat NARs serialized against each other, and `wave_run` used `join_all` so each wave cost its slowest member. One sliding window now covers everything, parts go eight wide inside it, bodies are an `Arc<[u8]>` or a file range instead of a `Vec` cloned per attempt, and HTTP/2 is on.

## Also fixed

- **The daily GC wiped the global edge cache.** The generation prefixed every cache key and the collector bumps it whenever a sweep deletes anything, so the 30-day `immutable` lifetime could never be reached. A stored object's key no longer carries it; only a cached absence does (ADR 0013).
- **Duplicate `Sig:` lines.** `with_signature` appended unconditionally and `nix copy` preserved existing Sig lines, so every push→substitute→re-push cycle added another. The live cache has narinfos carrying two today; it would have grown until the 64 KiB cap started failing pushes.
- **Worker settings.** `observability`, `placement: smart`, and `cpu_ms: 300_000` were all unset. Without the first, nothing about a slow read was diagnosable from production.
- **Build.** No `[profile.release]` and no RUSTFLAGS, so the wasm shipped without LTO or SIMD. Now 116 KB smaller with 6,259 vector instructions.
- Exponential backoff over five attempts instead of linear over three, and `WWW-Authenticate` on 401s.

## Breaking

A NAR write declares its decompressed size in `x-cachet-nar-bytes`, because the decoder needs a ceiling before the narinfo carrying `NarSize` arrives. Older clients answer 411. The bound is paired with a ratio cap on how far uploaded bytes may expand, so the decompression-amp defense is tighter than it was rather than looser.

## Dependency

The C zstd library enters `cachet-push` through a named wrapper in `deny.toml`, the same shape as the existing `ring` exception: ruzstd decodes and cannot encode, and the client has to produce the NAR it uploads. `cachet-push` and `cachet-cli` compile only for hosts. `check-wasm-hygiene.sh` now scans the artifact for `zstd_sys`/`ZSTD_` too, so the ban protects the bundle rather than the intention — verified green against the built bundle.

## Verification

Every local lane green: `unit` (185 tests), `property`, `golden`, `kani`, `workerd`, `deny`, `wasm-hygiene`, `clippy`, `clippy-wasm`, `openapi-check`, `doc-manifest`, `lane-manifest`, `scripts`, `fmt`.

The workerd lane gained assertions for the new contract: a NAR write without its declared size is 411, bytes that do not hash to the key naming them are refused and deleted, the facts document is unreachable from a request, re-pushing a signed narinfo leaves the signature list unchanged, and a stored object still answers from the edge under a corrupt generation while an absence does not. Its CLI scenario drives the real streaming client end to end, including a 100 MiB multipart payload.

What this does not prove is the deployment. `just destroy` and `just deploy` on a clean bucket, then `just integration`, and compare the post-step push against the 5 m 18 s baseline from run 32806212498 and the 31-minute `openapi` baseline from 32803263823.

## Not done

`cache_verdict` still awaits its KV write on the request path (`verdict.rs:326`), and the per-org membership loop is still sequential. Both are cold-isolate-only, and threading a `Context` through six call sites was a wider change than the rare path justifies.

I also tried holding the probe's bucket enumeration at the edge for a minute. It made things worse and is not in this PR: the memo drifts in the safe direction, but what it drifts away from is exactly the dedup that makes a warm push cheap, and the workerd lane caught a sibling push re-uploading paths it already had.
MD

Here's what I found and did while CI runs.

**Your instinct was half right.** Uploads are exactly as bad as you said. Downloads are not — I measured them.

| | cachet | cache.nixos.org |
| --- | --- | --- |
| narinfo warm / cold | 39 ms / 133 ms | — / 133 ms |
| NAR throughput | 38–42 MB/s | 50 MB/s |

Reads are at parity. They *feel* slow because **the cache is 4% full** — of 300 random local store paths cachet held 12, cache.nixos.org held 71. cachet is priority 30, so nix asks it first for every path in every closure, eats a 404, and goes upstream anyway.

The cache is empty because pushes don't finish. From run 32803263823:

| Job | Build | Push |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `openapi` | 47 s | **31 min** |
| `wasm` | 1 m 49 s | **18 min** |

Three causes, all fixed in [PR #18](https://github.com/nox-systems/cachet/pull/18):

1. **The worker re-read every NAR to verify it.** A narinfo PUT carrying 300 bytes triggered a full `bucket.get()`, a ruzstd decode, and two SHA-256 passes over bytes it had streamed past minutes earlier — 132 MB re-read and 541 MB hashed for one rustc path, ×3 on retry. Now measured by the write that stores it, recorded beside the object, and the narinfo reads the record. Verify-then-sign is untouched.
2. **`nix copy --to file://` compressed whole closures and threw them away.** Now one path at a time: `nix store dump-path` streamed through a zstd encoder, hashed as it passes. Nothing the cache already holds gets compressed.
3. **Multipart uploads ran in a sequential `for` loop** outside the concurrency waves, so the fat NARs serialized against each other. One sliding window now, parts 8-wide, bodies are refcounts instead of 90 MiB clones per retry, HTTP/2 on.

Two real bugs found along the way: the **daily GC wiped the entire global edge cache** (the generation prefixed every key), and **`with_signature` appended unconditionally** — your live rustc narinfo carries the same signature twice, and it would have grown every push→substitute→re-push cycle until the 64 KiB cap started failing pushes.

Two things I want to flag, since both cut against the plan:

- **I added the C zstd crate**, which `deny.toml` bans. ruzstd is decode-only and there's no usable pure-Rust encoder, so streaming `dump-path` was impossible without it. It goes in through a named wrapper the same way `ring` does, scoped to the two host-only crates, and I extended `check-wasm-hygiene.sh` to scan the bundle for `ZSTD_`/`zstd_sys` so the artifact is protected by a gate rather than a rule. Verified green.
- **I tried caching the probe's bucket enumeration and reverted it.** It drifts in the safe direction, but what it drifts away from is exactly the dedup that makes a warm push cheap — the workerd lane caught a sibling push re-uploading paths it already had.

Every local lane is green, including the workerd lane driving the real client end-to-end with a 100 MiB multipart payload. The wasm is 116 KB smaller with 6,259 SIMD instructions where there were none.

One breaking change: NAR writes now declare their decompressed size in a header, so older clients get 411. That's fine given you're wiping the deployment, and the action's pin is bumped to 0.4.0— sorry, 0.0.7.

I'll cut the release once CI is green and you've merged. What I can't prove from here is the deployment itself: after `just destroy` / `just deploy` on a clean bucket, `just integration` against the 5 m 18 s baseline is the number that settles it.

content.text:
Pushed to #19. Five consecutive local runs green.

On the flake — you're right that a deadline wait is not a structural fix, and I've dropped it. The real defect was that I asserted on a *count* across two requests with no synchronization point. The lane already had the right idiom and I didn't follow it: **wait for a positive event the request must emit, then assert what didn't happen.** The generation-zero scenario right below mine is that exact proof in the other direction. Mine now does the same, one request at a time, with the "no edge hit" claim made only after that request's own miss has landed. No counting, no new primitive, no retry. Every `doesNotMatch` in the file now sits behind an `untilEvent`.

**On the 411 — your read is exactly right, and it's my miss, not just a sequencing accident.** The action runs the pinned v0.0.6 binary, which doesn't send `x-cachet-nar-bytes`; the worker now requires it. I flagged this as "older clients answer 411" but treated it as a release-ordering detail when it's actually a rollout hazard: between deploying the worker and shipping the CLI, every job's push step fails and nothing gets cached. Jobs stay green because the action degrades, so it's silent.

Two ways out, and I'd rather you pick:

1. **Ship the release first, then deploy the worker.** No code change, but it constrains every future rollout of this pair and doesn't help anyone running an older pinned `cachet-version`.
2. **Make the header optional.** If it's absent, bound the decode by the expansion ratio alone — which is the bound that actually defends against a compression bomb; the declaration only tightens it. That removes the breaking change entirely, makes rollout order irrelevant, and keeps old clients working. It's maybe twenty lines plus a lane case.

I lean hard toward 2 — a cache whose upgrade order matters is a trap you'll hit again. Say the word and I'll add it to #19.

git tag -a v0.0.7 d69e8b8 -m "Version 0.0.7

The push path stops paying for its own bytes twice.

The worker measures a NAR on the write that stores it and records the
result beside the object, so signing a narinfo reads a few hundred bytes
instead of re-reading, decoding, and double-hashing the whole NAR.
Verify-then-sign is unchanged (ADR 0012).

The client serializes and compresses one store path at a time, streaming
nix's own NAR through a zstd encoder, so nothing the cache already holds
is compressed and discarded. Uploads share one sliding window with
multipart parts eight wide inside it, bodies are refcounts rather than
per-attempt copies, and the transport is HTTP/2.

A daily sweep no longer empties the edge cache (ADR 0013), a re-push no
longer appends a duplicate signature, and the worker deploys with
observability, Smart Placement, and a five minute CPU ceiling.

Breaking: a NAR write declares its decompressed size in
x-cachet-nar-bytes. Clients older than this answer 411, so upgrade the
action's cachet-version alongside any worker deploy." && git push origin v0.0.7 2>&1 | tail -3

Found it, and it's worse than a regression — **v0.0.6 had the identical failure and passed by luck.** Its x86-linux job hit the same `getrandom` error, but `cachet-cli` happened to finish linking before `cachet-worker` aborted the build, so dist found the binary. Adding zstd made `cachet-cli` slower to compile, so this time the abort won the race.

The root cause is that dist builds `--workspace`, which includes a crate that cannot build for a host by design.

**The staging deploy and integration lane both passed.** `staging` 2m28s, `integration` 2m17s — new worker, new client built from source, GitHub's real OIDC, nix verifying the signature on the round trip. The new protocol works end to end against a live deployment.

On the FlakeHub warning: `determinate-nix-action` is literally one step — `nix-installer-action` with `determinate: true` hardcoded. There's no input to keep Determinate Nix and skip the FlakeHub login. And the failure isn't really transient: it fires on every job because nox-systems isn't a FlakeHub customer, so the login can't succeed.

Which means the only real fix is to stop asking for it — and the repo has already half-decided that, since the composite logs out of FlakeHub immediately afterward with a comment saying every lookup would otherwise pay a wasted 401.

content.text:
What would you like to clarify?

For context on what's behind the question, here's what I actually verified rather than assumed:

- `determinate-nix-action`'s `action.yml` is a single composite step: `nix-installer-action` with `determinate: true` hardcoded. It exposes 24 inputs, none of which touch FlakeHub.
- `nix-installer-action` has exactly one relevant input, `determinate`, described as *"Whether to install Determinate Nix **and** log in to FlakeHub for private Flakes and binary caches."* One flag, both behaviours. There's no `flakehub: false` that keeps Determinate — the deprecated `flakehub` input just implies `determinate`.

So the coupling is upstream's, not something I can work around in our composite.

What I'm less sure of, and where you may know better:

1. **Whether losing Determinate Nix actually costs you anything here.** Our composite already logs out of FlakeHub immediately after install, so we're not using the one feature `determinate: true` buys. But you chose Determinate deliberately and may want its daemon/GC behaviour for consumers.
2. **Whether the netrc plumbing survives the swap.** The composite has a pointed comment that determinate-nixd's start-up synthesis of the netrc is "the only reliable one on these runners" — which reads like it was written after something else failed. If you hit a specific problem with plain `netrc-file` on GitHub runners, that's the thing that would sink the recommended option, and I'd want to know before proposing it.

content.text:
It doesn't solve it — `cachet-action` has the identical setup and would show the identical warning. Same `determinate-nix-action@v3.21.9`, same provision-then-logout dance.

But its comments are much more explicit than the in-repo copy, and they answer the thing I said I was unsure about:

> Determinate synthesizes the netrc the daemon reads at daemon start, merging every file under `additionalNetrcSources` — and that start-up synthesis is the only reliable one on these runners. **A later re-synthesis is gated on the FlakeHub login, whose transient failures otherwise leave cache reads at 401 and every build recompiling from source.**

So the write-config-before-install ordering isn't incidental — it's a deliberate defense against this exact FlakeHub failure. The warning you're seeing is the failure that design already survives. That's why builds stay green.

Which reframes the choice. It's not "warning vs. Determinate's benefits" — it's that **the entire netrc dance exists because of Determinate**, and dropping it removes the hazard rather than just muting the symptom:

| | Determinate (today) | `determinate: false` |
| --- | --- | --- |
| FlakeHub login | attempted, fails, warns | never attempted |
| Credential delivery | `additionalNetrcSources` + start-up synthesis, ordered before install | `netrc-file = /etc/nix/netrc` in `extra-conf` |
| Logout step | required | gone |
| Re-synthesis gated on FlakeHub | real hazard, worked around by ordering | doesn't exist |

Three things I'd still flag before you pick:

1. `nix-installer-action` with `determinate: false` still uses Determinate's *installer* — you keep the fast, reliable install, you just don't get Determinate Nix the product (its daemon management, its GC).
2. I haven't verified `netrc-file` via `extra-conf` on a real runner. It's standard nix and the old TS implementation used exactly that shape in `nix.custom.conf`, but I'd want a CI run proving the auth probe still reports 404 before calling it done.
3. Whatever you pick should land in both this repo's `action/` and `cachet-action`, or they'll drift.

Want me to prototype option 1 on a branch so we get a real CI signal on the probe, or would you rather keep Determinate and I file the unconditional-login behaviour upstream?

        else

        fi

        # doubles as the connectivity check: a cache that cannot answer its
        # public config fails the job here, before the build starts. The
        # retry only asks that "cannot answer" outlive a blip.
        public_key="$(curl -fsSL --retry 4 --retry-all-errors --retry-delay 2 "${CACHET_CACHE_URL%/}/api/public/config" | jq -r '.publicKey')"

        # caller's extra-trusted-public-keys line is parsed and dropped;
        # the invoking user must itself be trusted for the key to count.
        {
          echo "CACHET_EXTRA_CONF<<EOF_CACHET_CONF"
          echo "extra-substituters = ${CACHET_CACHE_URL%/}"
          echo "extra-trusted-public-keys = ${public_key}"
          echo "trusted-users = root $(whoami)"

Build only what dist ships, and stop asking FlakeHub for a login

Two CI defects, neither of them new.

dist builds `cargo build --workspace`, which includes cachet-worker: a
wasm32-only crate that fails a host build by construction, because its
manifest supplies getrandom under cfg(target_arch = "wasm32") and the
code names it unconditionally. That the release pipeline ever worked was
luck. Cargo keeps compiling in-flight units after a failure, so the run
succeeded whenever cachet-cli finished linking before cachet-worker
aborted, and failed when it did not. v0.0.6 hit the identical error and
passed; v0.0.7 failed once, then passed on a re-run with nothing changed.
`precise-builds = true` makes dist build `--package=cachet-cli`, which is
the only package it ships.

The installer logs in to FlakeHub on every job granting id-token: write,
which this action requires for its own OIDC token. This deployment is not
a FlakeHub customer, so the login cannot succeed: it warned on every job,
for every consumer, and the substituter it would have added answers 401
before every lookup falls through to cachet. There is no input that keeps
Determinate Nix and skips the login: determinate-nix-action is one step,
nix-installer-action with `determinate: true` hardcoded, and that input's
own description is "install Determinate Nix AND log in to FlakeHub".

So the action installs plain nix instead, which also deletes the
workaround the old shape needed. Determinate synthesizes the daemon's
netrc at start-up from `additionalNetrcSources`, and a later re-synthesis
is gated on the FlakeHub login, so a failed login could strand cache
reads at 401; the credential was written before the installer ran
specifically to dodge that. Plain nix reads `netrc-file` from its own
config, so the credential rides `extra-conf` with the substituter and the
trusted key, and the logout step and the config.json merge both go away.

`cachet setup` is untouched and stays Determinate-aware: it already
branches on whether the host runs Determinate Nix, registering the netrc
through `additionalNetrcSources` there and writing `netrc-file`
otherwise. A laptop installed the easy way keeps working.

gh pr create --title "Build only what dist ships, and stop asking FlakeHub for a login" --body "$(cat <<'MD'
Two CI defects, neither introduced by #18 — both were latent and #18 only changed the odds on one of them.

## The release pipeline was a coin flip

dist builds `cargo build --workspace`. That includes `cachet-worker`, which **cannot build for a host by construction**: its manifest supplies `getrandom` only under `cfg(target_arch = "wasm32")`, and CLAUDE.md §4 states the crate fails host builds and is excluded from `default-members`.

So every release run has been compiling a crate that errors. It passed anyway because cargo keeps compiling in-flight units after a failure — if `cachet-cli` finished linking first, dist found the binary and the job went green.

The evidence:

- **v0.0.6** (`32805833017`, x86_64-linux, *success*): same `error[E0433]: cannot find module or crate getrandom`, same two lines in `gc.rs` and `oauth.rs`.
- **v0.0.7** first attempt: same error, but `× failed to find bin cachet` — the abort won the race. Adding zstd to `cachet-push` made `cachet-cli` slower to compile, which is why it lost this time.
- **v0.0.7 re-run**: passed with nothing changed.

`precise-builds = true` makes dist build `--package=cachet-cli`. Verified locally:

```
building aarch64-apple-darwin target, using cargo profile dist --package=cachet-cli)
```

`cachet-worker` is never compiled.

## FlakeHub logs in on every job and cannot succeed

Every job in every consumer's CI prints:

```
Error: failed to update netrc via determinate-nixd: Login failure: Transient authentication mechanism error
##[warning]FlakeHub Login failure: The process '/usr/local/bin/determinate-nixd' failed with exit code 1
```

It isn't transient. On a runner granting `id-token: write` — which this action requires for its own OIDC token — Determinate mints a second token and logs in to FlakeHub. This deployment isn't a FlakeHub customer, so it can't succeed, and the substituter it would have added answers 401 before every lookup falls through to cachet.

There is no way to keep Determinate Nix and skip it. `determinate-nix-action` is a single composite step wrapping `nix-installer-action` with `determinate: true` hardcoded, and that input's own description is *"Whether to install Determinate Nix **and** log in to FlakeHub"*. One flag, both behaviours.

So the action installs plain nix (`determinate: false`), which also removes a workaround the old shape needed. Determinate synthesizes the daemon's netrc at start-up from `additionalNetrcSources`, and a **later re-synthesis is gated on the FlakeHub login** — a failed login could strand cache reads at 401 and send every build back to compiling from source. Writing the credential before the installer ran was specifically dodging that. Plain nix reads `netrc-file` from its own config, so:

| | before | after |
| --- | --- | --- |
| FlakeHub login | attempted, fails, warns | never attempted |
| Credential | `/etc/determinate/config.json` + `additionalNetrcSources` | `netrc-file = /etc/nix/netrc` in `extra-conf` |
| Logout step | required | gone |
| Re-synthesis gated on FlakeHub | real hazard, dodged by ordering | doesn't exist |

## `cachet setup` is untouched

The laptop path is independent of this and stays Determinate-aware — `crates/cachet-cli/src/setup.rs` already branches on whether the host runs Determinate Nix, registering the netrc through `additionalNetrcSources` there and writing `netrc-file` otherwise. Someone who installed Nix the easy way keeps working exactly as before.

## Verification

`dist plan` and a real `dist build --artifacts=local` confirm the `--package` invocation. `just actionlint` green (the two shellcheck notes in `release.yml` are pre-existing and in dist-generated output). The auth probe already in the action is what proves the netrc swap on a real runner: watch for `cachet: read auth probe returned 404` in this PR's jobs — 404 means authenticated, 401 means the credential didn't reach the daemon.

Done. v0.0.7 is published with all four archives, `v0` now points at `d69e8b8`, and [PR #20](https://github.com/nox-systems/cachet/pull/20) has both fixes.

On "zoom zoom" — partly, and worth being precise about it. This PR's jobs will download the 0.0.7 CLI, so you get the client-side wins immediately: no closure staging, streaming compression, the sliding window, HTTP/2, no per-retry body copies. But they push to `cachet.nox.so`, which is **still running the old worker** — production hasn't been redeployed. So the re-read-and-double-hash on every narinfo is still there. The full effect needs the production deploy.

Two findings from this round worth keeping:

**The release pipeline has never worked — it's been winning a race.** v0.0.6's x86-linux job hit the identical `getrandom` error and was marked success, because cargo keeps compiling in-flight units after a failure and `cachet-cli` happened to link first. Adding zstd made `cachet-cli` slower, so v0.0.7 lost the race, then won it on re-run with nothing changed. `precise-builds = true` builds `--package=cachet-cli` and never touches the worker crate.

**The FlakeHub warning isn't transient.** It fires because Determinate mints a second OIDC token and logs in unconditionally, and nox-systems isn't a FlakeHub customer. There's no input to keep Determinate and skip it — `determinate-nix-action` is one step wrapping `nix-installer-action` with `determinate: true` hardcoded.

The thing I'd watch in #20's logs: `cachet: read auth probe returned 404`. That line is the proof the `netrc-file` swap actually reaches the daemon — 404 means authenticated, 401 means it didn't. It's the one part of this I couldn't verify locally.

Name the CLI's Determinate Nix support where people look

The action stops installing Determinate Nix in this change, which makes
it worth stating plainly that the CLI's laptop path never depended on
that choice: `cachet setup` has always handled both installs, registering
the credential through `additionalNetrcSources` on Determinate and
writing `netrc-file` on plain nix, and restarting the daemon by whichever
route the machine has. That was only visible by reading setup.rs.

So the README says it, `cachet setup --help` says it, and the command
itself names which install it found before it lists the files it wrote. A
reader chasing a 401 needs to know which machine they are on before any
of those paths mean anything, and someone who installed Nix the easy way
should not have to guess whether this tool expects the other one.
